draft.title: The Western Front
card: The Western Front was the line of fighting across France and Belgium. Both sides dug lines of trenches, and the ground between them was called no man's land.
Australians reached the Western Front in 1916 after leaving Gallipoli. Early battles there included Fromelles in July and Pozières in July and August.
Machine guns could fire on troops crossing open ground, and artillery shelled trenches for days. Attackers were often cut down before they reached the enemy line.
The losses were huge. At Fromelles and Pozières thousands of Australians were killed or wounded in a short time, and living conditions in the trenches were also very hard.
draft.remember: On the Western Front, machine guns and artillery made attacks across open ground extremely costly.

a.q: Why were attacks across no man's land so costly for Australian troops in 1916?
opts: Machine guns and artillery fired on men in open ground
The trenches were too far apart for troops to reach
Australian troops had no training for trench fighting
The fighting took place only at night in thick forest
a.why: Machine guns and artillery could hit soldiers crossing open ground, so attackers were often cut down before reaching the enemy line. The distance alone was not the problem: the danger came from the weapons firing on them.
a.clue: Think about what the defenders could fire at men crossing open ground.

b.q: Which pair of battles did Australians fight on the Western Front in 1916?
opts: Fromelles and Pozières
Gallipoli and Fromelles
Pozières and the Suez Canal
Gallipoli and the Somme River
b.why: Fromelles and Pozières were both Western Front battles in France in 1916. Gallipoli was a different campaign, fought in 1915 against the Ottoman Empire, so any pair that includes it is wrong.
b.clue: One campaign in the wrong options was fought in 1915, not 1916.

wants.brief: A simple side view of the Western Front: two opposing lines of trenches labelled 'Allied trench' and 'German trench', with the ground between them labelled 'no man's land'.
wants.why: It shows what trenches and no man's land looked like, so the student can see why crossing open ground was dangerous.

a.best: Machine guns and artillery fired on men in open ground

problems.detail: The clue ('what the defenders could fire at men crossing open ground') repeats the wording of the right option ('fired on men in open ground'), so a student can match words without knowing the idea.

Pozières is given as 'July and August', but the Australian War Memorial dates the Pozières–Mouquet Farm fighting from 23 July to early September 1916. 'July to September' or 'from late July' would be more accurate.
